data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper, accessed October 2026
inflation_management: Inflation management improved markedly until geopolitics intervened. The 2006-2009 period ran hot at 9-14% on oil-boom overheating and the GFC; 2010-2013 moderated to 5.1-8.4% as the central bank moved toward inflation targeting (formal 4% target from 2015). The 2014-15 shock - oil crash, first sanctions wave, ruble devaluation - spiked inflation to 15.5% in 2015, followed by rapid disinflation to 2.9% in 2018, the credibility peak under Governor Nabiullina. The 2022 invasion drove it to 13.7% before emergency rate hikes (to 20%) and capital controls stabilized the ruble; but war spending has since overheated the economy - 5.9% (2023), 8.4% (2024), 8.7% projected 2025 - forcing the policy rate to a record 21% in late 2024.
debt_management: Russia's debt ratio is extraordinarily low - the standout of this group. It ran 7.4-12.3% of GDP in 2006-2013, rose only to ~13-15% after 2014, hit 19.2% in 2020, and is projected at 17.2% in 2025. This reflects oil windfalls saved in the Stabilization/Reserve and National Wealth Funds, conservative budgets, and - after 2022 - exclusion from Western capital markets forcing self-financing. The low ratio is real, but it flatters: it masks large drawdowns of sovereign wealth to fund the war and a budget increasingly dominated by military spending.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis: oil collapse and a sharp but brief recession; reserves deployed to defend the ruble.
Crimea annexation brought Western sanctions; oil crash and ruble float produced a 2015 recession.
COVID-19 plus the OPEC+ price war briefly drove oil futures negative.
Full-scale invasion of Ukraine: unprecedented sanctions (frozen reserves, SWIFT curbs, oil price cap), ruble collapse, then capital controls and a pivot of energy exports to Asia.
War economy: labor shortages, defense-led growth, persistent inflation, and National Wealth Fund drawdowns.

outlook_next_decade: Macro stability has been preserved through controls, energy revenues from non-Western buyers, and fiscal buffers - but at the cost of militarization and isolation. Over the next decade the risks are structural: sanctions persistence, sovereign-wealth depletion, demographic decline, and technological isolation dragging on productivity. Inflation is likely to run structurally above the pre-2022 norm, and the entire trajectory remains hostage to the war's outcome - the widest uncertainty band of the five.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
